food.text: In the Andes of South America, the potato was domesticated sometime between 8000 BC and 5000 BC. Beans, squash, tomatoes, peanuts and coca were domesticated there along with it.
In South America, agriculture began as early as 9000 BC, starting with the cultivation of several species of plants. Many of those first crops later became only minor ones.

Some scholars believe the earliest civilizations on the Peruvian coast first relied more on maritime resources than on agriculture. The Caral or Norte Chico civilization, dating back to 3500 BCE, is the oldest known civilization in the Americas.
Agriculture in South America may have begun in coastal Ecuador. The Las Vegas culture may have domesticated squash there about 8000 BCE.
Agriculture in South America may have begun in coastal Ecuador with the domestication of squash about 8000 BCE. The Las Vegas culture is credited with this early step.

Llamas, alpacas and guinea pigs are listed among the Andean domestications of the early period that also saw the potato tamed. Together with crops such as beans and squash, they shaped what the first Andean farmers ate.

Some of the earliest evidence of agriculture in South America is found in Colombia, dated to 4000 to 3000 BCE. Around then, hunter-gatherers left their rock shelters and began living on the open plains of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, especially the Bogotá savanna.

The earliest Andean civilizations arose on the hyper-arid desert coast of Peru. There, agriculture was possible only with irrigation in valleys crossed by rivers coming from the high Andes, plus in a few fog oases called lomas.

Lima butter beans, called pallares in Peru, have been part of Peruvian cuisine for at least 6,000 years. Today they are still served cooked whole, cooled and marinated in a salad with onion, tomato and green ají.

Cotton cultivated at Ancon, Peru, dated to c. 4200 BC, was the backbone of coastal cultures such as the Norte Chico. Cotton was grown upriver and made into nets. These were traded to fishing villages along the coast for large supplies of fish.

art.text: Early hunter-gatherers of the Lauricocha culture in central Peru made cave paintings of animals, hunting scenes and dances. The Lauricocha sequence runs from about 8000 to 2500 BC, before pottery was made in the Andes.
The earliest known surviving Andean textiles are samples of fiberwork from Guitarrero Cave in Peru, dating back to 8000 BCE. They show that weaving-related crafts in the Andes have very deep roots.

The Caral–Supe civilization of coastal Peru had no ceramics at all, and it also left almost no visual art. Alvaro Ruiz noted that its people made huge mounds and textiles, but almost no sculpture, carving or painting.
The early people of Lauricocha were skilled at working stone. The source calls their craft of making arrow points and fine blades sophisticated.

Early fiberwork by the Norte Chico people consisted of plant fibers that were intertwined and knotted into baskets and other containers. Surviving finely spun thread and simple cloths show that spinning and weaving were already well established and developed.
The arid desert of the Peruvian coast has preserved dyed textiles that can be 6000 years old. Many of the surviving samples come from funerary bundles.
Large-scale communal construction is clearly apparent in Caral–Supe from about 3200 BCE onward. The earliest date securely tied to a city is 3500 BCE, at Huaricanga in the Fortaleza area.

Early Peruvian gatherer-hunters moved between the rugged highlands and the coast, following wild animal herds and the seasons. Lauricocha, near Huánuco, was one of their important mountain encampments, and its people painted hunting scenes in caves.

Ruiz said that in the Norte Chico the interiors of the buildings are completely bare, with no bas-relief or drawing. He also said the lack of pottery went together with a lack of archaeologically apparent art, and that crops were cooked by roasting.

science.text: The Chinchorro, who lived along the Pacific coast of northern Chile and southern Peru, began artificial mummification by about 5050 BCE. This makes their mummies the oldest known examples of purposefully preserved human bodies in the world. The tradition lasted about 3,000 years, ending around 1800 BCE.
The earliest evidence of agriculture in the Andean region dates to around 9000 BC in Ecuador, at sites of the Las Vegas culture. The bottle gourd may have been the first plant cultivated there.

The oldest evidence of canal irrigation in South America dates to 4700 to 2500 BC. It was found in the Zaña Valley of northern Peru, and it shows early Andean farmers engineering the movement of water.

In 2008, a team led by Peter Fuchs announced a circular plaza of rocks and rectangular adobe bricks at Sechin Bajo. Radiocarbon dating indicated it was built in 3500 BCE, and a nearby 2-meter-tall frieze was dated at 3600 BCE. They are the two oldest examples of monumental architecture discovered so far in the Americas.

The black mummy technique, used from about 5000 to 2800 BCE, is the oldest of the main Chinchorro artificial mummification methods. The earliest examples come from the Camarones area on the Pacific coast of northern Chile. Preparing one meant taking the body apart: the skin was removed, then the soft tissue and internal organs, and the skeleton was disassembled. The bones were cleaned and put back in place with wooden poles, and the rebuilt body was coated with black manganese dioxide-based paint. Later black mummies found around Arica show the method becoming more elaborate.

The First Building at Sechin Bajo was reconstructed on five occasions, with plazas and staircases built, filled in and rebuilt. Calibrated radiocarbon dating puts it between 3700 BCE and 2900 BCE, before the use of pottery. Its sunken circular plaza feature was maintained throughout.

In February 2008, German and Peruvian archeologists working at Sechin Bajo uncovered a stone and adobe ceremonial plaza. They dated it to 5,500 years ago, making it the oldest known monument in Peru and one of the oldest structures ever found in the Americas.

politics.text: Caral–Supe, on the north-central coast of Peru, included as many as thirty major population centers. The first city is generally dated to around 3500 BCE at Huaricanga, and from 3100 BCE large-scale settlement and communal construction become clearly apparent. It is now recognized as the oldest-known civilization in the New World.

Scholars count six cradles of civilization, and coastal Peru's Caral–Supe civilization is one of the two earliest in the Americas, alongside the Olmec of Mexico. A civilization is defined by a state, social stratification, urbanization and symbolic systems. Caral–Supe may also have depended at first on marine resources rather than agriculture.

At Sechin Bajo, a plaza 10 to 12 meters across, built of rocks and adobe bricks, was dated to 3500 BCE. A nearby 2-meter-tall frieze was dated to 3600 BCE. A team headed by Peter Fuchs announced the find in 2008, and the two are the oldest monumental architecture found in the Americas.

At Sechin Bajo, the "First Building" was reconstructed several times between 3700 and 2900 BCE. The labor needed to build it implies a numerous sedentary or semi-sedentary population nearby. It also implies a mechanism of control to gather and supervise the workers.

No other site in the Americas has been found with such a diversity of monumental buildings, or such different ceremonial and administrative functions, as early as Caral. It lies in Peru's Supe District and is considered the oldest city in the Americas. UNESCO has declared it a Humanity Cultural Heritage site.

The earliest urban settlements of the Andes, as well as of North and South America, are dated to 3500 BC. They are Huaricanga, in the Fortaleza area, and Sechin Bajo, near the Sechin River. Both sites are in Peru.

Around La Galgada, archaeologists found at least 11 pre-ceramic settlements in the Tablachaca Canyon. Excavator Terence Grieder described the site as one of the most important ceremonial and burial areas of a well-populated district. He said it must be considered virtually a metropolitan center.

One skeleton at Caral, dated to around 3000 BC, is the earliest known evidence of human sacrifice in the Andean region. Some excavations have uncovered human remains associated with ceremonial or construction contexts, indicating that certain rites involved the deliberate killing of individuals. The skeleton's positioning and trauma, including skull fractures and finger mutilations, imply the person may have been a construction worker or a captive offered as a sacrificial victim.

One scholar sees patterns in Norte Chico that recurred later in Peru. They include the primacy of exchange over a wide area, a penchant for collective, festive civic work projects, and a high valuation of textiles and textile technology. Norte Chico is thus described as a cradle of later Peruvian civilization.

Some archaeologists propose a "maritime hypothesis": the rich resources of the Pacific let sedentary coastal societies flourish before irrigated agriculture began. Even so, by 3000 BC a sizable population in places like the Casma and Sechin valleys was building pyramids and other monumental structures, and it had no pottery.

culture.text: Early hunters in the Peruvian highlands left cave paintings of animals, hunting scenes and dances. They also worked stone with great skill, making arrow points and fine blades. These were the people of the Lauricocha culture.

Early Peruvian gatherers and hunters moved between the rugged highlands and the coastal areas. They followed the wild animal herds and the changing seasons. Lauricocha, near Huánuco, was one of their important mountain encampments.

The Chinchorro of the Pacific coast of northern Chile and southern Peru mummified men, women and children from across their communities. Elaborate funerary treatment was not restricted to a social elite. Deliberate mummification began by about 5050 BCE, making these the oldest known purposefully preserved bodies in the world.

Lauricocha Cave was discovered in 1957 at over 4000 m of altitude, near Lauricocha Lake. It held human remains dating back about 9,500 years to the last glacial period. They are the oldest found in Peru.

Early Paiján sites suggest large bands that moved seasonally between the coastal plains and the western slopes of the Andes. Most Paiján findings lie along the Jequetepeque, Cupisnique, Chicama and Moche river valleys of northern Peru.

The Valdivia culture is one of the oldest settled cultures recorded in the Americas. It grew out of the earlier Las Vegas culture and thrived on the Santa Elena peninsula in Ecuador between 3500 BCE and 1800 BCE.
The Lauricocha sequence is divided into three periods. Lauricocha I ran from 8000 to 6000 BC, Lauricocha II from 6000 to 4200 BC, and Lauricocha III from 4200 to 2500 BC.

French archaeologist Claude Chauchat identified dozens of open air Paiján sites, including camps, workshops and quarries. Chivateros is a notable prehistoric stone tool quarry associated with the Paiján culture.
Peruvian archaeologist Rafael Larco Hoyle first described the Paiján culture in the 1940s, working from the Pampa de los Fósiles site. The culture emerged on the northern coast of Peru.
